opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I didn't frame it as a business pitch at first. I framed it around timing.

I told WooSuk something like: "Look, vLLM has become infrastructure. Almost everyone serving open models touches it somehow. That kind of position doesn't come around often, maybe once in a career. If we don't build something around it now, someone else will, and they'll understand it less well than we do."

Part of it was about responsibility. When a project gets that big, the community keeps growing, but the core maintainers are mostly students or researchers doing this on the side. That isn't sustainable. Someone has to make sure the project stays healthy, stays open, and keeps up with new hardware and new model architectures. I said, "If we care about this thing, we should be the ones who make it last."

The other part was more personal. WooSuk is one of the people who really created vLLM. PagedAttention came from that early work, and he knows the system at a level very few people do. I told him the stakes weren't just "can we make a company work," but "do we want to watch from the sidelines while inference becomes one of the most important layers in AI, or do we want to shape it?"

I also tried to be honest about the risks. A startup is hard, and the open-source tension is real: you have to give a lot away and still find a way to create value. I didn't want to oversell it. But my feeling was that the downside of trying was manageable, and the downside of not trying was regret. I think that framing resonated with him more than any numbers would have.

r001.rationale: The response mentions the risk of vLLM failing to stay healthy and the regret of not trying, but it does not describe asking whether becoming wealthy would make WooSuk happy if vLLM failed because he chose not to join.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think I framed it as a sales pitch. WooSuk and I had been working together on vLLM for a long time by then, so he didn't need me to explain why the project mattered. What I tried to do was lay out, as plainly as I could, what I thought the next two or three years looked like.

The first thing I said was that inference was going to become the real battleground. Training gets the headlines, but every token that reaches a user has to go through an inference engine, and the cost of that is what decides whether a product survives. vLLM was already sitting at the center of that, and I felt that if we didn't shape where it went, someone else would, and probably in a way that served one company rather than the whole ecosystem.

The second point was about the project itself. Open source is wonderful, but a project at that scale can't run on evenings and weekends forever. Every week we were getting requests from hardware vendors, from model labs, from companies running it in production. If we wanted vLLM to keep its position, we needed people whose full-time job was to care for it. I told him that staying put was actually the riskier option, because the project would slowly lose the ability to keep up.

And the third thing, which was maybe the most personal, was that I said we were in a rare moment. Not many people get to build infrastructure that a large part of the industry depends on, with the community already trusting them. That window doesn't stay open. If we waited until things felt safe, the opportunity would have passed to someone else.

I don't want to overstate my role, though. He had been thinking about all of this himself. I think what I really did was put words to a decision he was already leaning toward, and make it feel less lonely to take the leap.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses vLLM’s stakes and says staying put could risk the project losing ground, but does not describe asking WooSuk whether becoming wealthy would make him happy if not joining caused vLLM to fail.

astra-6.text: I framed it as a choice between continuing vLLM as an open-source project and committing ourselves to building a company around it. The project was the starting point; the question was whether we wanted to take on everything that came next. I wanted WooSuk to see both the opportunity and the responsibility, because joining meant making a real commitment together.

r001.rationale: The response describes a choice between open-source work and building a company, but does not ask whether wealth would make WooSuk happy or connect his decision not to join with vLLM failing.

sol-6.1.text: I framed it as a chance to build something together around vLLM, with real uncertainty about whether it would work. The question was whether we believed in the opportunity enough to commit to it. I wanted WooSuk to feel like a partner in that decision.
